guides.summary: A watch combines a mechanism with choices about its appearance and story. ExplainerKit keeps those responsibilities separate so you can reuse a gear model in several explanations. guides.title: Runtime API
guides.summary: A scene keeps the shapes in an explanation together with the values and motion that determine their appearance. When you sample it at a chosen time, it calculates a frame without needing to play the earlier frames. A renderer draws that frame, while a player supplies the browser controls and clock needed to move between moments. This separation lets an animation and a reader interaction work on the same construction.

modules.responsibility: Native SVG scene rendering

guides.title: One model, explicit rendering choices
guides.summary: Keep scene identity, inputs, animation and geometry in ExplainerKit, then choose a renderer that can draw the representation your explanation needs. SVG and Canvas draw native 2D scenes, while spatial mathematics can project 3D line art into either one. Dense points and lines have a separate WebGL2 renderer. Use the optional Three.js adapter when you need supported solid or lit geometry and prepared 3D assets. Three.js does not become the scene model or the default renderer.

guides.title: Add depth and focus with layers
guides.summary: `drawing.layer({depth=1,bounds})` creates a root group with convenience `circle`, `rect`, `line`, `path`, `text`, `instance(component)` and `add(rootHandle)` methods. Children retain their ordinary identity, inputs and animation tracks. A depth can be a positive number or an input owned by this scene. Up to 32 layers are supported, with depth [.05,1000]. Nested depth layers refuse; ordinary groups inside them work.

guides.title: Refusing unsafe polygon samples and applying shape keys

modules.responsibility: Composition, motion, continuity, contrast, measured palette and 3D rendering diagnostics

guides.title: Composition audit
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/audit` while authoring to find potential layout problems in animated explanations. It can flag colliding text, marks drawn over words, low contrast, panels hiding other content, characters above their apparent floor and crowded frames. Like a linter, it points to places that need review rather than deciding whether the explanation works.

guides.title: Measure authored motion
guides.summary: Use `auditMotion` from `explainerkit/audit` to check the movement you have authored. Supply a function that returns a point at a requested time, whether that point comes from a scene object, a joint socket or a mathematical trajectory. You can then ask whether it stays still, follows a target, arrives at a chosen moment or remains below a speed or acceleration limit. The audit measures those requests directly and needs no reference clip or motion-capture data.

guides.title: Continuity and contrast audits
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/audit` to measure jumps when switching representations and text contrast over rendered pixels. These checks complement the composition audit, which works from scene geometry.

guides.title: Palette measurements and comparison
guides.summary: Use `auditPalette` from `explainerkit/audit` to measure how much of a rendered image each color occupies. You can also supply named groups of authored fills to compare the colors chosen for different parts of a scene. Capture pixels yourself before calling the audit, then use `comparePalettes` to compare two reports. These helpers inspect supplied data without drawing, reading the DOM, loading images, starting clocks or changing the scene.

guides.title: 3D rendering audit
guides.summary: A shaded 3D scene can look wrong in ways that are hard to spot until someone points at them. Fine parallel stripes can cover a curved petal, the edge of a tree's shadow can come out as a staircase, or two surfaces can flicker through each other. These artefacts come from a handful of renderer settings, and `explainerkit/audit` can check those settings before anyone has to find the artefact by eye. It can also look for stripes in a rendered image, which catches the cases a settings check misses.
headings: Look for stripes in the pixels
Audit a film or page automatically

modules.responsibility: Native WebGL point/line buffers

guides.title: Draw a large set of points and connections
guides.summary: Use the WebGL2 renderer for a dense field of observations, a network or a particle drawing whose positions are already supplied by your model. It draws point and line buffers using the graphics processor (GPU). A buffer is a typed array containing many values in a fixed order, which lets the renderer submit those values together rather than create one scene object per point.

The importer does not insert source markup into the page, adopt source DOM nodes, or fetch external resources. Once import succeeds, create an instance and use the part list to animate a named element as shown below.

modules.responsibility: Bounded static glTF/GLB geometry

guides.title: Bring a static model into line art
guides.summary: `importGLTF` reads the supported subset of glTF 2.0 or its binary form, GLB. It returns vertices in world coordinates and triangle edges without a direction. It does not require Three.js, load a library, fetch a URI or create a GPU context. The format and binary layout follow the [Khronos glTF 2.0 specification](https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html), especially nodes/transforms, buffers/views/accessors and GLB chunks.

modules.responsibility: Visual effects and color adjustments, with resource limits

guides.title: Shape the light and the surface
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/look` to add blur, glow, blending, gradient masks and color grading to ordinary scene properties. These effects change how a drawable appears without changing its geometry or the values it explains. SVG and Canvas use browser drawing and filter APIs through validated ExplainerKit settings, with no shader package, external resource URL or hidden rendering loop. Create your scene and drawable handles before applying the effects shown below.

modules.responsibility: Character runtime, faces, poses, walking and acting

guides.title: Characters
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/characters` to add a rigged character, give it actions and expressions, and connect it to live inputs. The module includes starter artwork, face and speech controls, planted-foot walks, pose tools, an audit and an SVG format artists can edit. Follow [Building a character that holds together](character-construction.md) to create a definition.
headings: Put a character in a scene

guides.title: Lightweight biped motion in 2D and 3D
guides.summary: `bipedMotion` calculates a walking pose at a requested time, including foot support and two-segment arm reaches. Use `bipedRig` to connect that pose to scene groups that hold your artwork. Both are optional character tools and neither starts a clock, creates a renderer or mesh, fetches resources, or manages the browser. The planar characters and `solveTwoBone` keep their documented behavior.

guides.title: Characters in profile
guides.summary: `profile(options)` creates a side-view biped definition, with an asymmetric nose/chin outline, one visible eye, an ear, and separately articulated near/far limbs. It shares the existing biped walk, run, pose, joint-goal and socket contracts. It does not turn a front-facing face into a profile by sliding its eyes.
headings: A live value drives a reaction

guides.title: Independent character timing
guides.summary: Scene tracks and rig parameters can already move at different times. A character’s `keys()` layers need extra care because a key that changes an elbow may also supply shoulder, hand and inverse-kinematics (IK) blend values to complete the limb pose. Use a channel mask when separate layers must control different joints.

guides.title: Keyed acting and track-driven travel
guides.summary: Schedule a pose when a character must arrive at a gesture at a chosen time, or supply a root track when it must travel along known positions. The example assumes an existing scene `s`, with `character` and `stick` imported from `explainerkit/characters`. Pose keys describe the gesture while `follow` supplies travel and foot planning.

guides.title: Quadruped gaits
guides.summary: A four-legged animal changes the order of its feet as it speeds up. It walks one foot at a time, trots with diagonal pairs and gallops with a moment when the feet are off the ground. `quadrupedGait` from `explainerkit/characters` plans those footfalls for a side view. It keeps each planted foot fixed on the ground, swings it on an arc to the next footfall and solves each leg as two bones. The plan is a pure function of time, so a scrubbed film and a live preview show the same pose.

guides.title: Play and synchronize a timeline
guides.summary: A timeline describes how named values change, while a timeline player supplies the clock that advances those values in the browser. Use `createTimelinePlayer` from `explainerkit/player` when your application already owns the objects being drawn and needs ExplainerKit to coordinate their motion. Your application receives the sampled values and applies them to its chosen renderer.

guides.title: Play native scenes through an existing renderer
guides.summary: Use `createProjectionPlayer` from `explainerkit/player` when you already have a renderer and want ExplainerKit to sample and play a native scene. Supply a projection callback that applies the validated frame to your renderer. The player evaluates scene tracks, parameters, derived values and camera projection using the same clock implementation as mounted SVG and Canvas players. It does not replace your renderer or create another animation engine.

modules.responsibility: Focused measured-label API

guides.title: Measured label placement
guides.summary: When points crowd together on a chart, a name that fits on the right of one point may cover the next name. Use `placeLabels` to assign a measured box to each label. The planner tries positions around each anchor, which is the point the label names. It also checks rectangular obstacles, such as the space reserved for the Moon in this star chart.

modules.responsibility: Focused annotation policy

guides.title: Place readable annotations around scene objects
guides.summary: Import `planAnnotations` from `explainerkit/layout/annotations`. It chooses label positions from measured rectangles in **CSS pixels**, after scene coordinates have been projected onto the screen. It does not alter scientific marks, narration, media time or a player's clock.

modules.responsibility: Sound generation and explicit playback

guides.title: Semantic sound for motion
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/sound` to design an effect, choose a musical voice or render a soundtrack tied to authored motion. The module generates numeric audio samples called PCM and accepts recordings that your application has already decoded. It shares the [mixer and WAV tools](audio-mixing.md) and [media playback adapter](sound-playback.md). Importing or rendering does not play audio, open a device, fetch assets or install a clock. Render the soundtrack first, then attach it to a player when a viewer requests playback.

guides.title: Audition an original soundtrack
guides.summary: Use `attachSoundtrack` from `explainerkit/sound` to play an already rendered soundtrack alongside a scene player. Prepare the decoded audio and the player first, then start playback from a user action.

guides.title: Procedural fields and instances
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/procedural` to generate repeated artwork from points and attributes. Start with `points` to choose positions, add properties with `attribute`, then draw them with `instance`. A `distribution` can turn measured samples into varied sizes or categories, and `noiseField` can vary a property through space and time. Every result is computed from an explicit seed, inputs and time without a separate animation loop, simulation history or runtime dependency.

guides.title: Density fields, network spacing and fractal noise
guides.summary: Use a density field to vary spacing across an area, a network to place points along connected paths, or layered noise to generate a repeatable scalar field. Each tool computes from explicit inputs and a seed. None installs a clock, fetches assets, reads the DOM or changes scene ownership. Choose the construction that matches your geometry before converting its points into scene artwork.
headings: Shared scalar fractals and domain warping

guides.title: Give data a visual meaning
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/data` to turn measurements and categories into positions, sizes and chart shapes. You can run these functions in Node.js or a browser without network access or third-party packages. Use their results in a scene’s data sources, parameters, derived values or bindings. Mount the scene in a browser to display the chart. Use `explainerkit/geometry` when the task is constructing a shape or arranging objects spatially rather than interpreting a measurement.

guides.title: Connected constructions
guides.summary: Build shapes from paths, repeat them along a curve, or connect measurements to their position and appearance. These tools work with SVG and Canvas. Use the sections below to choose an operation and understand its limits.
headings: Morph the outside and the opening

guides.title: Drawing, correspondence and batch sampling
guides.summary: Use `Line` to measure or trim a path, `samplePath` to place points along its visible length, `pairPoints` to match two point sets, and `inkStroke` to turn a centerline into a filled ribbon. Import them from `explainerkit/geometry`. They prepare geometry and data without creating a player, changing scene nodes or guessing the intended transition.

guides.title: Turn and split a 3D shape
guides.summary: Use `polyhedron` to draw a cube or an icosahedron as ordinary scene paths, so you can turn the shape or open a cut through it without adding a separate 3D renderer. A polyhedron is a solid enclosed by flat faces. The supported solids are convex, which means they have no inward dents and a straight line between any two interior points stays inside the solid.

They return ordinary paths or frames for SVG and Canvas and keep scene timing and application identities separate from geometric construction.

modules.responsibility: Procedural HSLA, safe conversions, hue-aware mixing and explicit RGB interpolation

guides.title: Color: procedural HSLA, explicit conversions
guides.summary: Use HSLA to create related colors by keeping a hue family while changing saturation, lightness or opacity. HSLA describes hue in degrees, saturation and lightness in percentages, and alpha as opacity. It is the preferred representation for new procedural color work in ExplainerKit. Use linear-light RGB instead when calculating lighting, combining pixels or measuring contrast.

modules.responsibility: Pure timelines, easing, staggering, motion paths, springs and secondary motion

guides.title: Schedule motion with a timeline
guides.summary: Use a timeline to describe how several named values change together. A **channel** is one of those named values, such as `dot.x`, and a timeline records the changes scheduled for each channel. It can return the values at any chosen time without owning a browser clock or changing your drawing objects directly.

guides.title: Reusable easing and staggering
guides.summary: Use staggering to decide when each object starts moving and easing to decide how it moves after it starts. A ripple provides one example of the difference. Points near the center start before points farther away, while every point can rise slowly, accelerate or overshoot its destination according to its easing curve. Changing either choice produces different motion without changing the objects themselves.

guides.title: Native spring timing
guides.summary: Use `springTiming` when a move should last until a spring has settled instead of using a duration chosen in advance. The helper samples the analytic spring model and returns a finite duration and easing function that you can pass to a scene track. Its times are seconds, and it owns no scene, DOM element, player or clock.
headings: Use the result with a millisecond clock

modules.responsibility: Seekable typewriter, object wipe, fly-in, pulse, teeter and colour flash presets

guides.title: Add a familiar animation effect
guides.summary: Use `commonEffect` to bring an object into view, reveal text, or briefly draw attention to a shape. Import it with `bindCommonEffect` from `explainerkit/motion/effects`. The same functions are also exported by `explainerkit/motion`.
headings: Own the binding and respect motion preferences

modules.responsibility: Scalar/vector fields, fractal/ridged noise, domain warp and deterministic grids

guides.title: Procedural fields and instances
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/procedural` to generate repeated artwork from points and attributes. Start with `points` to choose positions, add properties with `attribute`, then draw them with `instance`. A `distribution` can turn measured samples into varied sizes or categories, and `noiseField` can vary a property through space and time. Every result is computed from an explicit seed, inputs and time without a separate animation loop, simulation history or runtime dependency.

guides.title: Density fields, network spacing and fractal noise
guides.summary: Use a density field to vary spacing across an area, a network to place points along connected paths, or layered noise to generate a repeatable scalar field. Each tool computes from explicit inputs and a seed. None installs a clock, fetches assets, reads the DOM or changes scene ownership. Choose the construction that matches your geometry before converting its points into scene artwork.
headings: Shared scalar fractals and domain warping

modules.responsibility: Optional keyframe/timeline editing

guides.title: Edit animation keys and curves
guides.summary: Use the timeline editor when people need to adjust the timing and values of an animation that already exists in a scene. A key records a property's value at a particular time, and the segment between two keys describes how the value changes. The editor shows those keys and curves while the scene's player continues to own playback.

modules.responsibility: Connect authored values to HTML

guides.title: Animate the page you already have
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/dom` to apply scene values to existing HTML/CSS elements. Use `explainerkit/typography` to animate text that you can seek forward or backward on the same timeline. They use no third-party libraries, Web Animations timeline or independent animation-frame loop. SVG/Canvas remain the scene renderers; this is an additional browser adapter for ordinary page content.
headings: Split a phrase without losing its meaning

modules.responsibility: Explicit native browser animation

guides.title: Animate existing page elements
guides.summary: Use the Web Animations adapter when an existing HTML or SVG element needs to move or fade with browser animation. The Web Animations API, usually abbreviated WAAPI, is the browser's built-in system for describing these effects. ExplainerKit calls `Element.animate()` through `animateWAAPI` or `waapi.animate` from `explainerkit/adapters/waapi`.
headings: Share elements and recover from errors

modules.responsibility: Live observations, settled hover intent and reactive parameter/data bindings

guides.title: Live inputs and reactive scenes
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/inputs` to connect observations to scene parameters or table rows. A source captures an observation, a mapping turns it into the quantity you need, and a binding applies that quantity to the scene. Sources are available for pointers, resizing, files, device motion and orientation, cameras and microphones. Your application can also supply observations directly.

guides.title: Scroll cues and hover intent
guides.summary: Use a scroll cue when crossing a point in a story should change application UI, such as opening a panel. Use hover intent when a pointer should settle over an item before selecting it. Both adapters share the existing story, player or input-source lifecycle rather than changing scene sampling or starting devices. Your application supplies the cue's effects and the function that identifies an item under the pointer.
headings: Position crossings with explicit reverse policies

modules.responsibility: PCM mixing and WAV encoding

guides.title: Mix recorded audio and combine it with video
guides.summary: Import `createAudioMix` and `encodeWav` from `explainerkit/sound/mix`. Supply decoded mono or stereo pulse-code modulation (PCM) samples, not compressed bytes.

modules.responsibility: Synthesizer, plucked, struck, percussion and sampled instruments, an effect rack with equalisers, dynamics, reverbs and delays, and loudness meters

guides.title: Studio instruments
guides.summary: Use the instruments in `explainerkit/sound/studio` when a score needs more than a simple tone. The module builds synthesizer patches, plucked strings, struck bars and bells, a percussion kit and instruments made from your own recordings. Each one responds to how hard a note is played and how long it is held, and each can be placed on a track of a [produced score](music-production.md).

guides.title: Studio effects and meters
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/sound/studio` to shape decoded audio the way a mixing desk does. You can equalise a recording, control its dynamics, place it in a room, add movement or harmonic colour, and measure the result against a delivery loudness. The same effects run on every track, bus and master of a [produced score](music-production.md).
headings: Process a sound through a chain

modules.responsibility: Score composition and variations, MIDI exchange, arrangement in bars and beats, produced mixes with buses, returns, loudness targets and stems, song analysis, beat grids, retargeting and adaptive scores

guides.title: Music
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/music` to write instrumental music as editable data. This guide covers the score itself. You enter notes, repeat and vary phrases, exchange MIDI files with other software and render a stereo preview with the built-in voices. It also shows the modeled piano note in `explainerkit/sound`.

guides.title: Produce a score
guides.summary: Use `arrangeMusic` and `produceMusic` from `explainerkit/music` to turn written parts into a finished stereo mix. You write each part in bars and beats, assign it an instrument, route the tracks through effects and shared reverbs, and set the loudness the result should reach. The output is audio you can place under narration, with separate stems for an editor who wants to rebalance it.
headings: Write parts in bars and beats
How the documentary cues were made

guides.title: Time visuals to music
guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/music` to time an explanation to a piece of music. It can analyse a song your reader or your team supplies and report its beats, bars, chords, key, sections and moments such as drops and build-ups. It gives you a beat grid for snapping and pinning visual actions to those moments, and it can shorten or lengthen a song to fit an animation. For music you build from loops, it also plans a game-style adaptive score that changes state, layers and accents on the beat.
headings: Fit a song to your animation
Use beats from a neural tracker

guides.summary: Use `explainerkit/vfx` to track a feature or flat surface in recorded footage and composite graphics with foreground mattes or registered depth. For tracked annotations, analyze decoded frames and save positions indexed by clip time. During playback, sample those positions to move an ExplainerKit handle or another graphic.

modules.responsibility: Seeded, bounded and correlated differences between repeated things, with an audit for machine-made uniformity

guides.title: Organic variation
guides.summary: Repeated things look machine-made when every copy is identical, and they look chaotic when each copy is drawn from a wide uniform range. Real seeds, leaves and stones sit between those failures. Most copies are close to typical, a few differ more, related traits move together, and the occasional one is missing or out of line. `explainerkit/variation` gives each copy that kind of difference from a seed and its index, so the result is the same every time a frame is drawn.
headings: Give a row of seeds natural lengths and colours
Choose the shape of each difference

modules.responsibility: Draw the eye to a word, term or part while its context recedes, with one colour per topic

guides.title: Emphasis
guides.summary: An explanation often needs the reader to look at one word, term or part while the rest stays visible. Emphasis does that by treating the target and its context differently. The target takes an accent colour and can grow or lift slightly. The context recedes by fading and losing some colour, but it never disappears. `explainerkit/emphasis` describes that as a track of moments over time, so the same emphasis appears when a film is scrubbed, reversed or exported.
headings: Emphasise one word in a title
Hand emphasis from one target to the next

modules.responsibility: Live physical feel for interactive pages: soft chains, wind fields, spring followers, squash, pop, sway, tug, shake and hit-stop

guides.title: Juicy motion
guides.summary: Interactive pages feel alive when things respond physically. A stem bends in the wind the pointer stirs and springs back. A button overshoots and settles, and a seed lets go only after a visible tug. `explainerkit/juicy` provides those responses as small simulations you step yourself. The page supplies the time step and the inputs, so nothing here starts a clock or touches the page.

modules.responsibility: Regional projection, heightfields, hillshade, water flow, rivers, contours, draping, elevation colour, clouds and river reveals

guides.title: Relief maps
guides.summary: A relief map explains a place through its shape: where the high ground is, which way the water runs, and where the river cuts through. `explainerkit/maps` holds the geography for such a map. It projects longitude and latitude, samples and shades a heightfield, finds where water flows, traces rivers and contours, lays lines on the ground, colours by elevation and schedules a river being drawn on. Everything is a pure calculation. The module downloads nothing and draws nothing, so the application supplies elevation data and chooses a renderer.
headings: Turn a heightfield into shading and rivers
Project a region and lay a line on it

modules.responsibility: Lay text into document templates, find a phrase, map it onto a 3D page, and schedule its highlight and lift
keywords: lift a quote off the page

guides.title: Lift text from a page
guides.summary: Explainers often quote a source: a newspaper headline, a line from a book or a letter. A strong way to show it is to mark the phrase on the page and lift it off, so the words become the next part of the story. `explainerkit/typography/source` provides the calculations for that move. It lays text into a document template, finds the phrase, maps its position onto the curved 3D page and schedules the highlight and the lift. Each schedule is a pure function of time, so a film frame and a scrubbed preview always agree.

modules.responsibility: Film finishing on pixel buffers: tilt-shift, depth of field, bloom, halation, light rays, motion blur, lens distortion, grade and grain

guides.title: Finish film frames
guides.summary: A rendered frame often needs finishing before it looks filmed. A real lens blurs what is out of focus and spreads light from bright areas, and the result is usually graded and given grain. `explainerkit/vfx/post` applies those steps to a frame's pixels. It is meant for the film path, where each frame is rendered and exported one at a time, so it runs on the CPU and favours exact, repeatable results over speed.

Blur what is out of focus

pitfalls.message: For new VFX shots, prepare fitted camera poses with compileCameraTrack. Its standard level repairs isolated pose spikes by default. Choose strong for smaller spikes or none to inspect the original poses.
Text alignment is the `align` property with the values start, middle and end. `textAnchor` is SVG vocabulary and is rejected.
That easing name does not exist. Named easings are listed in vocabularies.easings, for example easeOut, easeInOut, smooth or linear, or pass a trusted progress function.
Text `align` takes start, middle or end, not center, left or right.
Path commands are absolute M, L, C, Q and Z only. Convert relative, smooth (S, T), arc (A) and horizontal or vertical (H, V) commands, or build paths with explainerkit/geometry.
The `glow` property is an object, not a number. See docs/modules/graphics.md.
A cloud takes `points: {positions: [x0, y0, x1, y1, …], radii?, colors?}`, not an array of {x, y} objects.
A band scale exposes `bandwidth` and `step` as numbers, not methods. Write `x.bandwidth`.
Create scenes with `scene({width, height})` from explainerkit/core. There is no global ExplainerKit object.
You rarely need your own animation loop. Animate with `to`, parameters or timelines and let `scene.mount()` return a player that owns the clock, so seeking and export keep working.

ExplainerKit has its own scales, timelines and effects. Check find_capability before adding another animation or charting library. Three.js is supplied to explainerkit/renderers/three, not imported by ExplainerKit.

Drawing directly to SVG or Canvas bypasses the scene, so seeking, export and audits cannot see it. Add shapes to a scene and mount it, or use a renderer from explainerkit/renderers/svg or explainerkit/renderers/canvas.
